persons.name: Bora Özkent
persons.digest:
Bora Özkent has two videos this weekend. In the Nasdaq video he argues that the sharp drops of the past two weeks come less from deteriorating AI fundamentals than from forced selling by leveraged and volatility-targeting funds; he says stocks like **NVDA** fell even as fundamentals improved, and semiconductors (**SOX**) are close to a bear market. He says his own portfolio is 15-16% below its peak of two weeks ago, that he still expects volatility to calm soon, and admits he missed a chance by not selling before the drop. He adds that the credit-side squeeze, such as pressure on **Oracle**'s credit ratings and **Meta**'s need to raise more funds, is no different from two weeks ago.

In the second video, published Sunday morning, he explains how AI will affect jobs and careers using the views of Stanford economist Erik Brynjolfsson: entry-level doors are narrowing for young people (under-25 unemployment in the US is 16%), management roles are more resilient, and the answer is to start using AI right away.

items.title: Who Will Get Rich and Who Will Be Jobless in the Age of AI?
items.summary: Bora Özkent explains how AI will affect jobs and careers through the views of Stanford economist Erik Brynjolfsson. AI differs from the industrial revolution because it boosts cognitive rather than physical production and spreads the tools to more people. In current data AI is not yet taking jobs but it is shutting young people out: under-25 unemployment in the US is 16% versus 4% overall. Companies used to hire young people and train them through apprenticeship, but now have AI do that work more cheaply. Management roles hold up better because they need approval, but the pressure is moving upward. Bora thinks things will get somewhat worse next year. His advice: start using AI right away, hand daily tasks over to it, build simple software, and develop in areas AI will struggle to touch, such as personal branding. He says the coming years could be great for those who adapt and terrible for those who do not.

items.title: Nasdaq Neden Aniden Sert Düşüyor (ve Sonra Sert Yükseliyor?)
items.summary: Bora Özkent argues that the roughly 3% index drops in the Nasdaq and semiconductors over the last two weeks, and pullbacks of 20-40% in some stocks, stem from forced fund selling rather than a fundamental problem. Earnings and growth expectations are very good; Nvidia's fundamentals improved while the stock fell very hard. The mechanism has three links: leveraged funds must sell as collateral erodes, automatic selling kicks in under risk budgets when volatility targets are exceeded, and short selling is rising (Goldman Sachs data). In the MSCI ACWI technology is 28% of weight but 40% of risk, and chips are 13% of weight but 20% of risk. He recalls that the collapse of a leveraged AI fund in July also hit the market. He says his own portfolio is concentrated solely in AI hardware, is down 15-16% from the peak of two weeks ago, and at one point had gains of 45-50% year to date. He says do not copy anyone else's portfolio; keep the stock if the shop's business is not deteriorating, but be careful if the debt is large or the technical break is severe. He expects volatility to calm soon and prices to return to old levels.

assets.note: Says its fundamentals keep improving, with revenue, profit and free cash flow growing, yet it fell very hard this week; he attributes this to fund selling.

items.title: AI narrative breaking...and Europe
items.summary: Defiant Gatekeeper groups his weekly market review into three headings. The S&P 500 fell 0.5% on the week, the Nasdaq 0.7% and the Dow rose 0.4%; the semiconductor index fell about 3.2%. Brent rose from $110 to $117 while the 10-year yield fell to 4.96%, the biggest one-day drop since March 2023; he reads this as the bond market betting against the economy. On Thursday the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 6.7%, Lam Research about 12% and Meta about 7%, while the S&P 500 rose about 0.7%, so this was an AI-stock selloff, not a crash. The triggers were Lam's supply-constraint comments and Meta raising its spending plan despite beating revenue expectations, with negative $2.1 billion free cash flow. He relays Jensen Huang's remark that the demand for capital is greater than its availability; CoreWeave and Nebius fell about 35% in two weeks and Anthropic's IPO valuation is said to have dropped to about $1.5 trillion. The high-yield spread is about 3.4%, so this is name-specific pressure, not systemic. The odds of a Fed hike at next week's meeting are 10% and above 75% for December; he speculates the tone might soften slightly. In the last section he says France's 10-year yield crossed 5%, the spread to Germany is the widest since 2011 and the problem is France-specific.

The guests see the rate decision as cautious and a clear cooling in demand, expect another 100 bps cut in December and see no growth recovery unless credit growth limits are loosened. On the US side Berk says bubble headlines come every three months and that the Broadcom CEO's remarks were misread; indebted companies that do not generate cash will struggle but every correction in strong tech is a buying opportunity. He says he added Energy Fuels on uranium, rare earths and the Wacker merger, finds SpaceX the right 5-10 year theme and keeps the Optimus theme on Tesla. He thinks CoreWeave will not go under, likes the stock and finds its 15% yielding bonds worth trying with 3-5% of a portfolio; for larger sums he suggests the near-10% yields on Turkish banks' dollar-denominated perpetual issues.
